chunks: Motor torque-speed, current and voltage curves. The question: Draw a torque vs RPM curve. What are its implications? Repeat for current and voltage vs torque and RPM.
Two simple rules describe a DC motor. Torque (its twisting force) is proportional to current, and back-EMF (the voltage it generates) is proportional to speed.
Put them together and the motor's behavior plots as straight lines. Torque is highest at zero speed and falls steadily to zero at the top speed.
Picture a rubber band pulling a toy cart.
The band pulls hardest when stretched the most, and the pull fades smoothly to zero as the cart reaches the spot where the band goes slack.
A motor's pull fades the same way: strongest when stalled, zero at its no-load speed.
The analogy has one gap: in a motor, changing the supply voltage slides the whole line, which a rubber band cannot do.
A straight line from stall torque (left) to the no-load speed (right). The midpoint is where mechanical power peaks.
The slope is the speed regulation: a motor with 4 times the winding resistance would sag four times as fast.
Drag the winding resistance to 8 ohms: the stall torque collapses to about 28 mN·m while the no-load speed barely changes.
Drag the supply to 15 volts and the stall torque and no-load speed both rise by about a quarter.
Torque ( T ): the twisting force the shaft delivers, in newton-meters (N·m). Torque constant ( K t ): how many N·m of torque you get per amp.
Back-EMF constant ( K e ): how many volts of back-EMF you get per rad/s (radians per second; one turn is about 6. 28 radians). Stall torque: the torque at zero speed, the maximum.
No-load speed: the speed where torque falls to about zero.
Take a 12 volts motor with 1 ohms winding and K t equals K e equals 0. 02 . Stalled, the current is 12 amps and the torque is 0. 02 times 12 = 0. 24 N·m .
The no-load speed is about 12 / 0. 02 = 600 rad/s . Halfway, at 300 rad/s, back-EMF is 6 volts, the current is 6 amps, and the torque is 0. 12 N·m, which is half.
The points fall on a straight line. That is the whole idea: one straight line between stall and no-load.
"With V equals IR plus K e omega and T equals K tI , torque falls linearly with speed from stall torque K tV over R at zero rpm to zero at the no-load speed V over K e .
Current is proportional to torque, so it's highest at stall and lowest at no-load. Back-EMF rises with speed, so the remaining voltage across the winding, IR , shrinks.
Peak power is at half stall torque and half no-load speed, but efficiency peaks at low torque near no-load speed, so you design to run in that region and never sit at stall."
